profile.profile: The Dances of Universal Peace (DUP) are a spiritual practice that employs singing and dancing the sacred phrases of the world's religions. Originating in North America in 1968 through Samuel L. Lewis, they combine chants, whirling, and participatory circle dancing. Facilitated by leaders using acoustic instruments like drums and guitars, the movement spans 28 countries.
profile.profile_long:
The Dances of Universal Peace (DUP) represent a global spiritual practice that combines group singing, sacred phrases from the world's religions, and participatory movement. Formulated originally in North America by Samuel L. Lewis, who was also known as Sufi Ahmed Murad Chisti, the practice emerged out of a rich synthesis of spiritual traditions. The very first dance took place on March 16, 1968, in San Francisco, California. Samuel Lewis drew profound inspiration from his spiritual relationships with modern dance pioneer Ruth St. Denis and Sufi master Hazrat Inayat Khan. While deeply influenced by Sufi traditions such as Sema and the practices of the Whirling Dervishes, Lewis was also a Rinzai Zen master, incorporating teachings from diverse faith backgrounds into a unified movement expression.

The physical format of a DUP gathering centers on community and shared participation rather than performance. Typically, anywhere from five to five hundred dancers stand together in a large circle. In the center of this circle stand a dance leader and musicians playing acoustic instruments. Spectating is largely discouraged because the primary objective of the gathering is joy, rather than the technical mastery or perfection of specific dance steps. A designated dance leader facilitates each session, frequently accompanying the singing by playing a drum, guitar, flute, or another stringed instrument. Because the dances are designed to be accessible, each dance is taught afresh at every gathering, allowing newcomers and seasoned participants alike to step in and follow along seamlessly.

Musically, the practice relies on a wide array of inspirational poetry, quotes, and sacred phrases drawn from global religious traditions. These texts are set to traditional, contemporary, or occasionally improvised melodies. Acoustic instrumentation provides a warm, organic soundscape where stringed instruments and percussion guide the collective breath. A deliberate choice is made to employ a diverse range of languages, including Arabic, Aramaic, English, Hawaiian, Hebrew, Persian, and Sanskrit. Dance leaders and promoters use these varied linguistic and religious elements to demonstrate that joy sits at the heart of every spiritual tradition. Participants experience the concept of the 'One Joy' through shared steps, chants, and multi-lingual expressions.

Over the decades, the DUP movement expanded far beyond its initial countercultural roots. Originally performed at camps and alternative gatherings carrying a distinct New Age feel, the dances have increasingly found a home in diverse environments. Today, they are offered in traditional places of worship as well as secular and institutional settings, including schools, colleges, prisons, hospices, residential homes for individuals with special needs, and holistic health centers. Furthermore, the therapeutic applications of the dances and the walking meditations developed by Samuel Lewis have been explored across various clinical and community settings.

The global institutionalization of the practice advanced significantly with the establishment of the International Network for the Dances of Universal Peace in 1982. Founded by Neil Douglas-Klotz and Tasnim Fernandez—who served as teachers in the Sufi Ruhaniat International and Sufi Order International respectively—the network helped anchor and spread the movement worldwide. Both founders remain leading exponents, and Douglas-Klotz's creation of dances utilizing the Aramaic words of Jesus has successfully integrated into both alternative and mainstream religious circles. Presently, the network maintains active members across twenty-eight countries, ensuring the continuous transmission of Lewis's vision.

The underlying philosophy of the DUP emphasizes inclusivity and spiritual development. Participants of all ability levels, including children, dance together in an environment that fosters spiritual awareness, hand-eye-body coordination, and the competency of harmonizing with others. Dancers engage in coordinated gestures, sometimes whirling in a manner reminiscent of dervish practices, while maintaining spatial awareness within the living perimeter of the circle. Many individual dances feature specific choreography, movements, steps, and gestures designed to encourage dancers to explore the deeper mystical meanings embedded within the sacred phrases. Through this unique combination of breath, sound, and circle movement, the Dances of Universal Peace continue to cultivate an embodied experience of interfaith harmony and global community.

sections.origins_and_history: The Dances of Universal Peace were first formulated by Samuel L. Lewis, also known as Sufi Ahmed Murad Chisti. The very first dance took place on 16 March 1968 in San Francisco, California. The original dances were strongly influenced by Samuel Lewis's spiritual relationships with modern dance pioneer Ruth St. Denis and Sufi master Hazrat Inayat Khan. Sufi practices such as Sema and The Whirling Dervishes provided clear influences, alongside Lewis's background as a Rinzai Zen master. Originally performed at camps and alternative meetings, the movement expanded into schools, prisons, hospices, and holistic centers. The International Network for the Dances of Universal Peace was founded in 1982 by Neil Douglas-Klotz and Tasnim Fernandez, and the network now has members in 28 countries.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Five to 500 dancers stand in a circle, often around a leader and musicians with acoustic instruments in the center. All dances are participatory and spectating is somewhat discouraged because joy is the goal. Dances are facilitated by a dance leader who often plays a drum, guitar, flute, or other stringed instrument. Each dance is taught afresh at each gathering, allowing dancers of all levels and children to follow along. Many dances feature choreographed movements, steps, and gestures encouraging dancers to explore deeper mystical meanings.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music relies on chants put to traditional, contemporary, or occasionally improvised melodies using inspirational poetry, quotes, and sacred phrases. Facilitators play acoustic instruments such as drums, guitars, flutes, or other stringed instruments in the center of the circle. A wide range of languages are deliberately employed, including Arabic, Aramaic, English, Hawaiian, Hebrew, Persian, and Sanskrit.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dances were originally performed at camps and meetings with a distinctly New Age and alternative feel. Over time, they have increasingly been offered in diverse places of worship and more secular places such as schools, colleges, prisons, hospices, residential homes for those with special needs, and holistic health centers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The intention of the DUP is to raise consciousness and promote peace between diverse religions. Dance leaders tend to believe peace can be promoted through experiencing the same One Joy through diverse dance steps, chants, and languages. Dancing is seen as an opportunity to develop participants' spiritual awareness, hand-eye-body coordination, and competency in harmonizing with others.
sections.notable_figures: Samuel L. Lewis (Sufi Ahmed Murad Chisti) formulated the dances. Ruth St. Denis and Hazrat Inayat Khan influenced Lewis's work. Neil Douglas-Klotz and Tasnim Fernandez founded the International Network for the Dances of Universal Peace in 1982 and became leading exponents.
sections.regional_variants: The dances have developed into a global movement with members in 28 countries. Neil Douglas-Klotz's creation of dances using the Aramaic words of Jesus has entered many alternative and mainstream religious circles.
sections.lineage: The tradition is of North American Sufic origin, drawing significant influence from Sufi practices such as Sema and The Whirling Dervishes, modern dance pioneers like Ruth St. Denis, and Rinzai Zen teachings.
